title: WPSS/3820/2018 of KM. RANJITA RANA Vs STATE OF UTTARAKHAND

paras.text:
WPSS No. 3820 of 2018
Hon'ble Manoj K. Tiwari, J.
Mr. Ghanshyam Joshi, Advocate for
the petitioner.
Mrs. Seema Sah, Brief Holder for the
State of Uttarakhand.
Mr. M.S. Bhandari, Advocate, holding
brief of Mr. Pankaj Purohit, Advocate for
respondent nos. 2 & 3.
Mr. Niranjan Bhatt, Advocate, holding
brief of Mr. Vinay Kumar, Advocate for the
applicants in impleadment application
(CLMA No. 2835 of 2019).
Heard learned counsel for the parties.
According to the petitioner, she
belongs to O.B.C. Category and she is also
entitled for horizontal reservation available
to Uttarakhand Women. Petitioner
participated in a selection for the post of
Village Panchayat Development Officer in
District Uttarkashi. Result of the said
selection was declared on 04.10.2018, in
which petitioner secured 54% marks.
Grievance of the petitioner is that
certain persons, who have secured lesser
marks than her, were called for verification
of documents, meaning thereby, they were
treated as successful; while, petitioner,
despite scoring more marks, was not called
for verification of documents. Thus, feeling
aggrieved, petitioner has filed this writ
petition seeking the following reliefs:

"(i) a writ of mandamus commanding
the respondents to declare the
petitioner select/qualify and call the
petitioner for verification of document
on the basis of her merit i.e. 54 marks
secured by her for the post of Village
Panchayat Development Officer (code
of post 04R) Uttarakhand Women

category in the department of
Panchayati Raj in District Uttarkashi
for which the cutoff marks is 48
marks."
A counter affidavit has been filed by
the Selecting Body, namely, Uttarakhand
Subordinate Service Selection Commission.
Paragraph no. 3(D) of the counter affidavit
is extracted below:
"3(D). That from the aforesaid
breakage of the posts, it is evidently
clear that in District Uttarkashi there
was no post available to be advertised
for the O.B.C. Category. The petitioner
submitted her candidature as an
O.B.C. category candidate in District
Uttarkashi. The cut-off marks for
General (Open) category is 62 and for
General (Women) category the cut-off
marks is 48. Admittedly the marks
obtained by the petitioner is 54 which
is less than the marks obtained by the
General (Open) category candidate i.e.
62. It is for this reason, the petitioner
could not make it to the merit list of
General (Open) category in District -
Uttarkashi. The contentions of the
petitioner that the cut-off marks of the
General (Open) category candidate is
48 is wrong and incorrect."
Learned counsel appearing for
Uttarakhand Subordinate Service Selection
Commission has placed reliance upon
Government Order dated 18.07.2001,
which provides that horizontal reservation
will be available to a person in his/her
category. He submits that, since there was
no vacancy on a post reserved for O.B.C.
category, therefore, petitioner, who belongs

to O.B.C. category, cannot be considered
against open category. He further submits
that petitioner cannot get reservation
available to Uttarakhand Women in open
category.
I am not impressed by the submission
made on behalf of the respondents. A
Constitution Bench of Hon'ble Supreme
Court in the case of Indira Sawhney &
others Vs Union of India reported in 1992
Supp (3) SCC 217 has held that reserved
category candidates, who get selected in the
open competition field on the basis of their
own merit will not be counted against the
quota reserved for them and they will be
treated as open competition candidates.
Paragraph No. 811 of the said judgment is
extracted below:-
"In this connection it is well to
remember that the reservations
under Article 16(4) do not operate like a
communal reservation. It may well
happen that some members belonging
to, say Scheduled Castes get selected
in the open competition field on the
basis of their own merit; they will not
be counted against the quota reserved
for Scheduled Castes; they will be
treated as open competition
candidates."
Similarly, in the case of Gurmeet Pal
Singh Vs State of Punjab reported in
(2018) 7 SCC 260, Hon'ble Supreme Court
has held in para 12 of the judgment that it
is settled position in law that persons
belonging to the reserved category, who get
selected in open competition on the basis of
their merit, have a right to be included in
the general/unreserved category and are
not to be included in the quota reserved for
that Category.

Similar view was expressed by Hon'ble
Supreme Court in the case of Tripurari
Sharan & another Vs Ranjit Kumar
Yadav reported in (2018) 2 SCC 656,
pertaining to admission in educational
institutions.
Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of
Alok Kumar Pandit Vs State of Assam &
others reported in (2012) 13 SCC 516,
while considering the right of a reserved
category candidate for appointment against
unreserved post has held as under:-
"24. As a sequel to the above, the
questions framed in this appeal are
answered in the following terms:
24.1. A reserved category candidate
who is adjudged more meritorious than
the open category candidates is entitled to
choose the particular service/cadre/post
as per his choice/preference and he
cannot be compelled to accept
appointment to an inferior post leaving the
more important service/cadre/post in the
reserved category for less meritorious
candidate of that category.
24.2. On his appointment to the
service/cadre/post of his
choice/preference, the reserved category
candidate cannot be treated as appointed
against the open category post."
Sub-Section (6) of Section 3 of the U.P.
Public Services (Reservation For Scheduled
Castes, Scheduled Tribes and Other
Backward Classes) Act, 1994 also provides
that if a person belonging to Scheduled
Caste, Scheduled Tribe or Other Backward
Classes gets selected on the basis of merit
in an open competition with general
candidates, he shall not be adjusted against

the vacancies reserved for such category
under Sub Section (1).
There is no dispute that petitioner
belongs to State of Uttarakhand, therefore,
she is entitled to the benefits available to
Uttarakhand Women. Hon'ble Supreme
Court in the case of Tirpurari Sharan
(Supra), while dealing with the question of
admission of a meritorious reserved
candidate against unreserved seat, has held
as under:-
"8. Often, in a competitive
examination held for the purpose of
admission in technical and medical
institutions, etc. some candidates
belonging to reserved
category/categories, qualify for the higher
ranking on the basis of their own merit
and depending on their performance in
the common entrance test, are placed in
the general merit list. Such class of
candidates belonging to reserved
categories who qualify on their own merit,
to be placed in general merit list, are
described, for the purpose of convenience,
as Meritorious Reserved Candidate (MRC).
It is by now well settled that an MRC who
goes on to occupy a general category seat
is not counted against the quota reserved
for a reserved category candidate, but is
treated as an open competition candidate
or general merit candidate. This Court in
Indra Sawhney v. Union of India has
observed thus: (SCC p. 735, para 811)
"811. In this connection it is well to
remember that the reservations under
Article 16(4) do not operate like a
communal reservation. It may well
happen that some members belonging
to, say, Scheduled Castes get selected

in the open competition field on the
basis of their own merit; they will not
be counted against the quota reserved
for Scheduled Castes; they will be
treated as open competition
candidates."
9. Even in service matters, the same
principle is made applicable. The
aforementioned principle of Indra
Sawhney is followed for admissions to
seats in medical colleges, and the same
was followed in R.K. Sabharwal v. State
of Punjab. However, the issue before us is
more nuanced - whether MRC can opt for
a seat earmarked for reserved category?
"If answer is yes" then since MRC
exercises the option of admission to the
seats in different colleges earmarked for
reserved category candidates, should a
less meritorious reserved category
candidate who is affected by such
process be given admission to the college
left over by MRC consequently?
10. This would be better understood
by a simplified example. Let it be
assumed that there are 100 seats
available through one common entrance
examination to PG courses in various
medical colleges across the country. Of
these, 50 are general category seats and
the remaining 50 are reserved category
seats. X, a reserved category candidate,
is assigned rank number 50 on account of
his performance in the entrance
examination. Thus he is just above the
cut-off for reserved category candidates,
and has got an open merit rank. Hence, X
is an MRC; however, X being in general
category is not willing to accept the seat
available for general category at the time
of his counselling. He wants admission in

another college of his preference which is
incidentally reserved for reserved
category candidates, and a seat in the
same is available in the reserved
category. Consequently, X chooses a seat
available in the college meant for reserved
category candidate based on his merit
among the reserved category candidates.
As he does so, one seat in the general
category list of 50 candidates remains
unoccupied. In that context, two questions
arise for consideration:
(i) Whether X-MRC can opt for a
seat earmarked for reserved category?
(ii) If answer is yes; what happens
to the 50th seat which was to be
allotted to X-MRC (i.e. 50th general
merit candidate) had he opted for a
seat meant for the reserved category to
which he belongs?
11. This Court has repeatedly,
including the judgment in Indra
Sawhney, concluded that the aggregate
reservation should not exceed 50%.
Therefore, even when an MRC opts for
a seat reserved for reserved category
candidates, caution has to be exercised
to maintain the reservation to 50%. So
also it is not open for the authorities to
deny an MRC a seat in the college of
his preference based on his merit, if
such seat is available at the relevant
point of time and the same is reserved
for candidates of the reserved category
to which the MRC belongs. This is
because there may be instances where
an MRC may not get a seat in the
institution of his choice on the basis of
his own merit in the general merit.
Under such circumstances, he may opt
to be treated notionally as a candidate

belonging to the reserved category only
for the purpose of getting a seat in the
college reserved for reserved category
students. If such MRC is to be placed in
the reserved merit list of his category,
he would be ranking high and may get
better choice of institution or course. An
MRC cannot be placed in a
disadvantageous position by not
permitting him to be treated as
reserved candidate, as that would
amount to making him suffer for his
better performance in the competitive
examination."
In view of the law laid down by
Hon'ble Supreme Court, a reserved category
candidate can compete against unreserved
post by virtue of his/her superior merit.
Therefore, reliance placed by the
respondents upon Government Order dated
18.07.2001 is misconceived. The said
Government Order does not prohibit a
reserved category candidate from being
considered against open category post.
In such view of the matter, the writ
petition is allowed. Respondents are
directed to consider petitioner's claim for
appointment as Uttarakhand Women
against an unreserved post, within four
weeks from today.
There will be no order as to costs.
 (Manoj K. Tiwari, J.)
Arpan 29.03.2019
